title: Writing that actually happens
desc: From a labeled diagram to a lab conclusion. Why the blank page is the problem, word banks and frames, the two-minute quick write, feedback on one thing, and what a good level-two paragraph looks like.

cues.text: Every Teacher, from EL Publishing. Marcus and Elena. Episode five, writing. Elena, I give a writing prompt, and my English learners write nothing. Or two sentences. What's going on?

Two things. One, writing is the slowest domain to develop, for everybody, in every language. Speaking comes first, writing comes last. So a student who is a level three in speaking is very often a level two in writing, and that's normal. Two, the blank page. A blank page with a prompt at the top is the hardest possible writing task. There's no vocabulary, no structure, no model. It's the writing equivalent of saying, go talk for five minutes, with no question.
So how do I take the blank off the page?

Three things on the page before they write a word. A word bank: the eight or ten words they'll need, right there. A frame or a structure: first, then, finally, for a process; claim, evidence, reason, for an argument. And a model: one paragraph that you wrote, about a different topic, so they can see the shape without copying the content. Word bank, frame, model. With those three, a level two writes a paragraph. Without them, nobody does.
Let's level it. What does writing look like at each level, in a biology class?

Level one: labels and lists. Label the diagram. List the four parts. Copy the sentence and change one word. That's writing. It counts. Level two: sentences from frames. The nucleus controls the cell. The membrane blank the cell. Three or four of those, and you've got a paragraph. Level three: a short paragraph with a word bank and a structure, and they fill in their own sentences. Level four: a paragraph with a model but no frames, and you're pushing on connectors: because, however, as a result, which means.
I think my mistake has been giving everyone the level four task and wondering why the level ones didn't do it.

And the fix isn't a different assignment. It's the same assignment with a different amount of scaffolding on it. Everyone writes about the cell. The level one labels it and writes two frame sentences. The level four writes the paragraph. On the same rubric, everyone can hit proficient on the content.
Talk to me about quick writes. I've heard you push these.

Two minutes, every day. End of a lesson, or after a chunk of talk. One question, one frame, two minutes, pencils moving the whole time, spelling doesn't count. Today I learned that blank. The most important part of the cell is blank because blank. And then, crucially, read one or two out loud, or have partners swap and read. Low stakes, high frequency. A student who writes two minutes a day in your class writes more in a semester than they would from three big essays, and they do it without fear.
Feedback. I bleed red ink all over these and I'm not sure it helps.

It doesn't. A level two student who gets back a paragraph with fourteen corrections learns one thing: don't write. Pick one. One thing per piece. This week, it's capital letters at the start of sentences. Next week, it's using because. Mark that one thing, say it in person, and let the rest go. The rest will come. And when you do mark it, give the correct version, not just a circle. A circle says you're wrong. The correct sentence says, here's how it goes.
What about grammar? Do I teach it?

You don't. The EL teacher does. What you do is notice the grammar of your subject and name it. Science writes in the passive: the solution was heated. History writes in the past and uses because a lot. Math writes with if and then. Point those out once in a while. Here's how a lab conclusion sounds. Here's a sentence that explains cause. That's not grammar class, that's just showing what biology writing looks like.
Give me a good level-two paragraph. So I know what to be happy with.

Here's one. The cell has a nucleus. The nucleus controls the cell. The cell has a membrane. The membrane protects the cell. The mitochondria makes energy. Five sentences, from frames, correct content, correct grammar. That's a level two doing exactly what a level two should do. If you got that from a student who wrote nothing in August, that's a win, and you should tell them so.
I would've marked that as too simple.
It is simple. It's also correct, and it's biology, and it's in English. Next month, you add because. The cell has a membrane because it needs protection. Then you've got a level three.
Stop worrying about?

Stop worrying about spelling in a first draft. And stop worrying when a student writes a word in Spanish in the middle of an English sentence. That's not a mistake. That's a student who knows the idea and hasn't got the word yet. Write the English word above it and move on.
Last episode next time: assessing fairly, and the people who can help you. Every Teacher, from EL Publishing, free at radan55 dot github dot io slash everyteacher.
